## Overall project summary (end-of-course goal)

::: callout-note
This section describes where your project ends up **at the end of the course**.
It is not the to-do list for this milestone: see [Milestone 2 summary](#milestone-2-summary) for that.
:::

In this course you will work in assigned teams of three
or four (see group assignments on GitHub) to answer a predictive statistical/machine learning question
using a publicly available data set that will allow you to answer that question.
To answer this question, you will perform a complete data analysis in R and/or Python,
from data import to communication of results,
while placing significant emphasis on reproducible and trustworthy workflows.

By the end of the course, your project will have evolved from a single,
monolithic Quarto document into a fully reproducible and robust data analysis project, comprised of:

-   a well documented and modularized scripts written in R and/or Python,
-   a data analysis pipeline automated with GNU Make,
-   a reproducible report powered by Quarto,
-   a containerized computational environment created and made shareable by Docker
-   a remote version control repository on GitHub for project collaboration, sharing, and documentation.

## Milestone 2 summary

1.  Move your project's computational environment into a container:
    build its image on GitHub Actions for both Intel/AMD and ARM computers,
    publish it on Docker Hub,
    and work in it from now on.

2.  Publish your report on GitHub Pages.

The reference for this milestone is
[docker-uv-renv](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv),
the example project the textbook's Containers chapters build up to.

### 1. Use a container for the computational environment

Once this section is done,
shift the development of your project from working in a virtual environment to working in a container.
The chapters to read are
[Python and R in one image](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-uv-renv.html)
(and the uv and renv chapters before it),
[Docker Compose](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-docker-compose.html),
[Working in a container over ssh with Positron](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-ssh-positron.html),
and [Building images for several platforms](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-platforms.html).

#### i. Start from docker-uv-renv's `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml`

Copy the [`Dockerfile`](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv/blob/main/Dockerfile)
and [`docker-compose.yml`](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv/blob/main/docker-compose.yml)
from docker-uv-renv into the root of your repository.
Its image has R 4.6.2, Python packages installed with uv, R packages installed with renv,
Quarto for rendering your report,
and an ssh server so you can work in the container from Positron.
Keep the Compose service's name, `analysis-env`,
so the commands below work as written.

Then remove the language your project does not use from the `Dockerfile`:

::: panel-tabset
## Python only

Delete the R packages part:

-   the `RUN echo "RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library" ...` line
-   `COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./`
-   `COPY renv/activate.R renv/`
-   `RUN Rscript -e "renv::restore()"`
-   `libuv1-dev` in the `apt-get install` list (only the R package fs needs it)

Your project has no `DESCRIPTION`, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile` or `renv/`.

## R only

Delete the uv part, but keep `WORKDIR /workspace`:

-   `COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/`
-   `ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv`
    and the `RUN echo "UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=..."` line after it
-   `COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./`
-   `RUN uv sync --locked`

Your project has no `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` or `.python-version`,
and you render with `quarto render` instead of `uv run quarto render`.

## Python and R

Keep both parts.
:::

**Note - the `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.**

#### ii. Your environment files

The image installs your packages from your lock files,
so these files must be in your repository and agree with each other:

-   **Python (uv):** `pyproject.toml` with each package pinned to an exact version (`==`),
    `uv.lock` and `.python-version`.
-   **R (renv):** `DESCRIPTION` with each package pinned to an exact version (`(== x.y.z)`),
    `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile` and `renv/`.
    `DESCRIPTION` is required in this milestone
    (see [renv: declaring packages in `DESCRIPTION`](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/virtual-environments-r-renv-description.html)),
    and it must list `knitr` and `rmarkdown`:
    Quarto uses these two packages to run the R code in your report.

To add a package, follow the chapter for your language
([uv](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-uv.html),
[renv](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-renv.html)),
commit the changed files together,
and let GitHub Actions publish a new image.

#### iii. Build and publish the image on GitHub Actions, for both kinds of computers

Add a GitHub Actions workflow, `.github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml`,
that builds your image for both `linux/amd64` (Intel/AMD) and `linux/arm64` (ARM, such as Macs with Apple silicon)
and pushes them to Docker Hub as one image,
tagged `latest` and with the commit SHA.
It should run whenever a push changes the `Dockerfile` or a lock file,
and when you run it by hand.
Start from the two-platform workflow in
[Building images for several platforms](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-platforms.html),
and change only its `IMAGE` line, to your Docker Hub repository's name, all in lowercase.

For the workflow to push,
one team member creates a public Docker Hub repository for the project
and a Docker Hub [access token](https://docs.docker.com/security/access-tokens/) with Read & Write permissions,
and adds two [repository secrets](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets)
to your GitHub repository
(Settings \> Secrets and variables \> Actions \> New repository secret):
`DOCKER_USERNAME`, the Docker Hub username,
and `DOCKER_PASSWORD`, the access token (not the Docker Hub password).
This is the same as in Individual assignment 2,
where you built for one kind of computer.

Check that the run succeeds,
and that your image's tag on Docker Hub lists both `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`.

#### iv. Run the container with Docker Compose

In `docker-compose.yml`,
use your published image instead of building it,
pinned to the commit-SHA tag your workflow pushed
(for example, `image: yourname/yourproject:sha-1a2b3c4`), not `latest`.
When your workflow publishes a new image,
update the tag in a pull request.

Keep the ssh setup from docker-uv-renv:
the port, `2222:22`,
and the mount of `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`.
Work in the container with Positron over ssh, as in
[Working in a container over ssh with Positron](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-ssh-positron.html).

#### v. Document the container in your `README`

Your `README`'s instructions for running the analysis must now use the container,
in this order:

1.  Make an ssh key if you don't have one: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`,
    pressing Enter at each question.
    Without the key,
    Docker makes a folder named `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` in its place,
    and ssh into the container fails until you delete that folder and make the key.
2.  Download the image: `docker compose pull`.
3.  Render the report in the container:
    -   Python, or Python and R: `docker compose run --rm analysis-env uv run quarto render`
    -   R only: `docker compose run --rm analysis-env quarto render`

    Add your report's path after `quarto render` if your project has no `_quarto.yml` that lists it.
4.  Work in the container: `docker compose up -d` starts it in the background,
    then connect with Positron over ssh;
    `docker compose down` stops it.
5.  Update the container:
    add a package with your environment manager,
    commit and push,
    wait for GitHub Actions to publish the new image,
    then update the tag in `docker-compose.yml` and run `docker compose pull`.

::: callout-important
## Your README instructions are worth 5 all-or-nothing points

5 points of this milestone are for the reproducibility of your README instructions:
whether someone can follow them to launch your container and run your analysis in it.
These points are all-or-nothing.
If your instructions do not work exactly as you have written them,
you will lose all 5 points.

Make sure your instructions work on both Windows and Mac computers.
If your team does not have both,
work with another team to test them.
:::

### 2. Publish your report on GitHub Pages

Anyone should be able to read your report online,
without cloning your repository.
You learned to publish with GitHub Pages in DSCI 521
([Introduction to Quarto and GitHub Pages](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/quarto-github-pages.html)),
where you published a whole Quarto website.
Here you apply those skills to publish the HTML version of your report.

::: callout-note
## Already published your report in Milestone 1?

Switch to the setup below, even if your current one works.
Later milestones build on it.
:::

You publish by hand, with a small workaround.
It works because of how GitHub Pages serves files:

-   GitHub Pages can publish the files in a `docs/` folder on your `main` branch, exactly as they are.
-   When someone visits your site's address, the web server shows the file named `index.html`.
-   With `embed-resources: true`, your rendered report is a single HTML file
    that holds everything it needs, including its figures.

So publishing your report is just putting a copy of that one file at `docs/index.html`.
Copying files by hand is easy to forget, so it is not how you would publish a larger site.
Later in the program (in DSCI 524, when you build websites for your packages),
you will use tools that build and publish a website for you.

1.  Make your rendered report a single, self-contained HTML file,
    with `embed-resources: true` in its HTML options,
    for example in the report's YAML header:

    ```yaml
    format:
      html:
        embed-resources: true
    ```

    If your project's `_quarto.yml` already sets this, you don't need to add it again.
    A self-contained file holds its figures and styling,
    so it still works after you copy it somewhere else.
    If you have only been rendering your report to PDF, render it to HTML as well.

2.  Render your report.
    Then copy the rendered HTML file into a `docs/` folder at the root of your repository,
    and name the copy `index.html`:

    ```bash
    mkdir -p docs
    cp <path-to-your-report>.html docs/index.html
    ```

3.  Add an empty `.nojekyll` file to `docs/`,
    so that GitHub Pages serves your file exactly as it is
    (see [Turning off Jekyll with `.nojekyll`](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/quarto-github-pages.html#nojekyll)):

    ```bash
    touch docs/.nojekyll
    ```

4.  Commit and push `docs/`.
    It is a copy of a generated file,
    but GitHub Pages can only publish files that are in your repository.
    Check that your `.gitignore` does not ignore `docs/` or `.html` files.

5.  In your repository on GitHub.com, go to **Settings > Pages**.
    Under **Build and deployment**, choose **Deploy from a branch**,
    then the `main` branch and the `/docs` folder, and click **Save**.

6.  After a few minutes, your report is published at
    `https://ubc-mds-2026-27.github.io/<your-repository>/`.
    Open it and check that the whole report shows, including its figures.

7.  Put this URL in your `README` (as the link to your rendered report)
    and in the **About** section of your repository.

::: callout-important
## Keep the published report up to date

`docs/index.html` is a copy.
Each time you re-render your report,
copy it into `docs/` again and push,
or the published version will fall behind.
We grade your work from your `1.0.0` release,
and the report on GitHub Pages should match it.
:::

## Submission Instructions

Just before you submit the milestone 2,
create a release on your project repository on GitHub
and name it something like `1.0.0` ([how to create a release](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository#creating-a-release)).
This release allows us and you to easily jump to the state of your repository at the time of submission for grading purposes,
while you continue to work on your project for the next milestone.

Follow the instructions for submission on Gradescope.
We only need URLs, entered into Gradescope directly: there is no PDF to make.
You will submit:

1.  the URL of your project's GitHub.com repository
2.  the URL of a GitHub release of your project's GitHub.com repository
3.  the URL of your report on GitHub Pages
4.  the URL of your image on Docker Hub

## Expectations

-   **Everyone should contribute equally to all aspects of the project** **(e.g., code, writing, project management).**
    **This should be evidenced by a roughly equal number of commits,** **pull request reviews
    and participation in communication via GitHub issues.**
-   Each group member should work in a [GitHub flow workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/quickstart/github-flow);
    where they create branches for each feature or fix,
    which are reviewed and critiqued by at least one other teammate
    before the the pull request is accepted.
-   You should be committing to git and pushing to GitHub.com every time you work on this project.
-   Git commit messages should be meaningful.
    These will be marked.
    It's OK if one or two are less meaningful, but most should be.
-   Use GitHub issues to communicate to their team mate (as opposed to email or Slack).
-   Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense.
    It doesn't have to be complicated.
-   You should use proper grammar and full sentences in your README.
    Point form may occur, but should be less than 10% of your written documents.
-   You will not be expected to incorporate Milestone 1 feedback in this submission (of course you can, but likely you will not receive it until the end of the week which might be too late to incorporate it).
